problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{-{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-2t}} & =\frac{1}{s+2},\,s>-2 \\ L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}-L{{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)-(s+2)}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =\frac{-6}{(s+2)(s-4)} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(s+2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{-2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-2,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{4t}}$ is defined for $s\in (4,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(-2,\infty )\cap (4,\infty )=(4,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>4.$
